title: The river that came down
hookLine: Bhagiratha brings the Ganga down from heaven and Shiva catches her in his hair; why a drop of Ganga water purifies the puja cup
carry: the ganga came down to purify
last: GHANTA — THE BELL IS A CALL: COME.

lines: BURNED TO ASH BY A SAGE.
ONLY THE GANGA CAN FREE THEM.
cards: King Sagara had sixty thousand sons, and he sent them all to find a lost sacred horse. They dug through the earth looking for it, and found it grazing beside a sage deep in meditation, Kapila.
They called him a thief and rushed at him. He turned on them, and they were burned to ash.
For generations their ashes lay there, and nothing could free them, except, the wise said, the Ganga, the river of heaven, if she would come down to earth. Kings tried and failed.
Then their great-great-grandson, Bhagiratha, gave up his throne and prayed for years, until the river agreed. One problem: a river falling from heaven would smash the earth.

teach.h: SHIVA CATCHES THE RIVER IN HIS HAIR.
teach.b: So Shiva stood beneath her and caught the whole river in his matted hair, and let her out gently, in streams. Bhagiratha drove ahead in his chariot, and the Ganga followed him all the way to the ashes.
Her water touched them, and Sagara's sons were freed and rose to heaven. That's the Ramayana's telling, and it's why images of Shiva show a little river spilling from his hair.
Even now, in Hindi, a huge effort is called Bhagiratha's effort. Here's the teaching. For Hindus, the Ganga isn't just a river.
She's Ganga Ma, a goddess and a mother, and her water purifies.
That's why so many Hindu homes keep a small bottle of Ganga water, Ganga jal, often brought back from a pilgrimage. A drop goes into the puja cup. It's sprinkled to make a place or a person ready.
A little is given to someone who is dying, and ashes are carried to the river, the way Sagara's sons were freed.

teach.h: THE SMALL CUP ON YOUR SHELF.
teach.b: And the small cup on your shelf echoes it every morning. Before puja, many people sip a little water from the palm, to begin clean. Water is offered to wash God's feet and hands, like a guest's.
Then it comes back to the family, a few drops in the palm, as a blessing. The plainest thing on the shelf carries the biggest river.

how: Many Hindus keep a small vessel of Ganga water (Ganga jal) at home, add a drop to the puja water, sprinkle it to purify, and give a little to the dying; in puja, water is offered to the deity as to an honored guest, sipped by the worshipper to begin clean, and received back afterward as a blessing.

games.why: a drop of Ganga jal goes into the puja water. the river came down from heaven to purify, and a drop carries that into the morning.

practice: With a small cup of water, or at a sink, wash your hands slowly, as if you were about to greet someone you honor. Then pour a few drops somewhere as a gift: a houseplant, the soil outside, the cup in your corner.
If you pray, you can say Ganga's name, or a name you honor, as the water goes. Then take one small sip and notice it: washed, given, received, the way the river came down.

wordCard.voice: The water. In puja it washes, it's offered, and it comes back as blessing; and a drop of the Ganga, the river that came down, makes it holy.

orig.note: Sanskrit jala: water. In Hindi it's said JUL; Ganga jal is Ganga water.

carryVoice: Your line: the Ganga came down to purify. Shiva caught her so she wouldn't break the world. One hundred fifteen days now.
